newsitem.title: UK: BARCLAYS SEES NO FURTHER CONCESSIONS ON PAY.
newsitem.headline: BARCLAYS SEES NO FURTHER CONCESSIONS ON PAY.

text.p: British banking group Barclays Plc said on Thursday it does not foresee making further concessions to staff unions in a dispute over pay.
"We've already made some quite considerable and rather expensive concessions and we don't think we need to make any more really," Barclays chief executive Martin Taylor told Reuters in an interview.
He was speaking after Barclays announced an eight percent rise in pre-tax profit in the first half of this year to 1.376 billion pounds.
Earlier, one of the unions representing Barclays staff urged the bank to resume pay negotiations after talks to avert a dispute broke down earlier this week.

"The (Barclays) directors and shareholders can expect to do well out of the profits announced today but over half of the staff...will receive no increase in salary for the foreseeable future," Banking Insurance and Finance Union (BIFU) negotiating officer Jennifer Cole said in a statement.
Taylor said support for any industrial action by the unions was small, "Only a small number of staff have voted in favour of it."
Barclays has said it is prepared to talk to the unions but would not re-open negotiations in a dispute linked to performance-linked pay, which will affect some 60,000 members of staff.
Staff at the bank are due to start an overtime ban within the next two weeks in protest at the pay proposals, which the union said, would impose a pay freeze on 25,000 staff.

The date for the start of the overtime ban would be set next week, BIFU said. The unions expected the overtime ban to severely disrupt business and delay customer accounts and transactions. Cash machines were also likely to be affected.
Barclays said it expected the impact of the industrial action to be "minimal".
BIFU is co-ordinating the dispute with another union UNiFI. UNiFI said on Monday it would go ahead with industrial action after the bank broke off talks with it and BIFU.
Talks broke down after just two days, when the bank refused to refer a pay-and-grading structure dispute to the government industrial relations arbitration service ACAS.
Taylor said the bank was trying to move away from a 1950s-style pay structure where staff "are paid more for getting older."
He said there is no fundamental disagreement with the staff on the need for the new scheme but that the arrangement for the transition period covering the change is still at issue.

"We've already moved out to a three-year phase-in, and honestly that's enough," Taylor added. "We know this is hard for some staff and we've given it a lot of thought and done a lot of consultation. The staff have been brilliant, we wouldn't have come up with figures like this without what the staff have done."
